THE ACTUAL WORKSHEET

Exactly what you’ll print.

This is the real sheet — the same file the buttons above hand you. Title, instructions, the activity itself, and a grown-up answer line where it helps.

The PDF is a real printable file (A4, prints fine on US Letter). The print button prints only the worksheet — never the website around it. No sign-up, nothing stored.

ABOUT THIS WORKSHEET

What your child practices.

Predicting endings is the comprehension move strong readers make automatically, and this sheet rehearses it three times: seeds bloom (not bicycles), flour bakes (snowmen need not apply), and helmets mean riding. Each wrong ending is a lovely “why not?” conversation.

  • Predicting story endings
  • Cause-and-effect endings
  • Rejecting silly endings
  • Story vocabulary
HOW TO USE IT

Three easy steps.

  1. Tell the story together

    Read the title and instruction aloud, then let your child point at the picture and say what happens. The picture carries the whole activity — no reading needed.

  2. Mark the picture, then retell

    Circle, number or draw on the sheet exactly as the game plays on screen. Afterwards ask “can you tell me the whole story?” — the retelling is the comprehension.

  3. Use the draw box

    Every sheet ends with room to draw the next part of the story. A drawing plus one spoken sentence is a complete session.

TEACHING TIPS

Little things that help.

Wrong answers are information

If the story comes out in the wrong order, retell it together and try again tomorrow. Comprehension grows from talking, not from being right first time.

Say the WHY out loud

“Why does Rabbit need the umbrella?” Asking for the reason turns a matching task into real story thinking.

Print it twice

Once to do, once to keep. Children love redoing a favorite story a week later and feeling how easy it got.

Answer guide

Row 1 = A (a flower blooms). Row 2 = B (a pie bakes). Row 3 = A (a ride down the path). In the printed art the fitting endings sit at A, B, A — the online game mixes them.
